extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of psychology, psychoanalysis, and literary/language criticism; readers interested in the mechanics of humor and wit
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and describe the formal techniques by which wit is produced (linguistic mechanisms, stylistic operations, and their psychological economy), illustrated with literary and anecdotal examples. Focus is on taxonomy of techniques and the common principle that unites them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condensation (with mixed word-formation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A form of condensation in which two ideas are combined into a single expression by mixing word elements (mixed word-formation), producing an abbreviated phrase that hints at both thoughts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and explanation: mixed compounds or portmanteau-like formations condense two thoughts into one expression; the condensatory formation is a substitutive formation that leaves a trace in wording. Compare to other condensation types; see Freud's examples of blended words and references to dream condensations (Autodidasker—Autodidakt and Lasker).

rubrics_metrics.name: Condensation (with modification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Condensation produced by a slight modification of an existing expression (change of a letter, word, or small element) so that the omitted or suppressed thought is evoked by the altered form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: changing tête-à-tête to tête-à-bête to evoke 'bête' (stupid ass); 'great future behind him' (replace 'before' with 'behind'); 'four heels of Achilles' (implies animality). The technique relies on omission plus a small substitutive modification; the less significant the modification, the stronger the wit. Condensation with modification is contrasted with mixed word-formation but may overlap.

rubrics_metrics.name: The whole and the part (word-division/charade)
rubrics_metrics.description: Using the same word first as a whole and then as its divided syllables or parts so that the syllables yield a different meaning (word-division or charade-like play).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Rousseau → roux et sot; Buona parte → Buonaparte. Technique: one and the same proper name or word is used in two applications in the same utterance (whole then parts) to produce wit. If substitution of the name removes the wit, the effect depends on the sound/structure of that specific word.

rubrics_metrics.name: Change of order (exchange of phrases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Using the same material of words but slightly changing their order so that the same words yield a different sense when re-arranged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: ‘Put in a dinner and a speech appears—put in a speech and a dinner appears.’ Technique: a small permutation (exchange of places) makes what was said of one person apply, by inversion, to another; useful in repartee and contrastive jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slight modification (near-identity change)
rubrics_metrics.description: Using the same material with a very small modification (one letter or phoneme) to produce a differentiated meaning while preserving sound similarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: antesemitism → antisemitism (one letter change produces retort); Traduttore—Traditore. The modification can be barely noticeable in careless pronunciation; this yields a powerful associative effect. Related to condensation-with-modification but used without condensation when the full sentence already states the thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Same words used in full vs colorless sense (full vs grammatical element)
rubrics_metrics.description: Using a word first in its full, meaningful sense and again in a colorless/grammatical sense (or vice versa) so that the same surface words carry different semantic weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: unremitting → un + remitting (prefix 'un' read as negation vs as phonetic segment); undertaker → 'one who undertakes' vs funeral manager; ‘carry out’ taken literally. Technique exploits derivative forms or suffix/prefix that are semantically 'colorless' in some uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Name and verbal significance (double-meaning of names)
rubrics_metrics.description: Double meaning derived from a proper name that also has a verbal/paraphrasable significance, or by a name resembling ordinary words, producing two compatible senses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: puns with names in Shakespeare (Pistol), Heine and other literary quips where a name carries both identity and a verbal/readable component. If the unchanged name cannot be used, slight modification can achieve the double meaning (Elsa → Alsace example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Metaphorical and verbal meaning (double application)
rubrics_metrics.description: Double meaning obtained by using a word that has both a literal/verbal sense and a metaphorical sense within the same utterance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'holding the mirror up to nature' (author/father with laryngoscope holding a mirror); satire 'biting' example. Technique leverages the coexistence of literal instrument/act and metaphorical literary function.

rubrics_metrics.name: True double meaning / play on words (ideal case)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cases where one word, as it stands, legitimately and naturally expresses two meanings simultaneously—no division, modification, or substitution needed (a word functioning in both senses in-situ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'C’est le premier vol de l’aigle' (vol = flight/theft); 'Le roi n’est pas sujet' (roi/subject double reading). This is the ideal manifold application: both meanings are genuinely available in context and give rise to wit without extra manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguity (double-meaning with uncertain dominance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Double meaning where both senses are plausible and the listener cannot decisively prefer one sense over the other; often leads to sexual innuendo in examples noted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'The army does not believe in her innocence' — innocence = legal innocence vs sexual innocence. When both senses are equally applicable the ambiguity itself generates wit. Distinguish from cases where one sense clearly dominates and merely alludes to the other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double meaning with allusion (one sense obtrusive; other veiled)
rubrics_metrics.description: Double meaning where one sense is more prominent/obtrusive and the other is veiled or suggested (allusion), so the wit depends on the concealed secondary sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'This satire would not have been so biting had the author had more to bite' (metaphoric/primary reading dominates but alludes to another); sexual allusions where the sexual sense is veiled. Freud calls this 'double meaning with allusion.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Tendency to economy (economy as chief category)
rubrics_metrics.description: The unifying principle of various wit techniques: a compressing or economic tendency in expression that preserves or implies an additional thought by saving wording—'thrift' in expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument and examples: economy explains condensation, manifold application, plays on words—wit economizes by packing two ideas into one expression. Examples: 'gold mine / gold spoon / gold cure' conveys multiple generations economically. Caveat: economy alone is not sufficient for wit (not every brevity is witty); must be a particular form of economy attendant to wit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brevity of wit (special kind vs mere laconism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Wit depends on a special kind of brevity—conciseness that results from a technical process (condensation/manifold application), not mere shortness of expression (laconism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observation: brevity alone does not guarantee wit; many laconic expressions are not witty. The brevity of wit often arises from a subordinate process (e.g., substitutive formation) that leaves a specific trace in wording, producing the pleasure of wit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Puns (sound-based, 'lowest' form)
rubrics_metrics.description: Puns rely on similarity of sound between two distinct words rather than identity of a single word's two senses; often regarded as the cheapest or lowest form of wit because they demand little technical effort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: humbug; cæsars → cæsuras; Calcutta/Calcutta roast example cited as poor pun. Puns typically change vowels or exploit rhythmic/phonetic similarity. K. Fischer's distinction: pun = bad play on words (plays with sound, not word-meaning). Puns are a subspecies of play-on-words but less esteemed technically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Displacements (witticisms resisting classification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Witticisms whose techniques are not easily classified under previous groups; they may involve shifting reference, ironic correction, or layered semantic shifts that defy neat taxonomy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Heine's 'Golden Calf' reply — 'he must be older than that' (correcting 'Golden Calf' → implies 'Golden Calf' is older than nineteenth century idol-worship); K. Fischer reads this as play on words but Freud notes such examples baffle classification. These 'displacements' show the taxonomy has limits and some witticisms rely on context-sensitive associative shifts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy to dream condensation (dream-work parallel)
rubrics_metrics.description: Processes similar to wit's condensation are observed in dreams (the dream-work), where latent thoughts are transformed into manifest dream-content by condensation and substitutive formations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freud's comparison: dream-work condensation produces analogous mixtures of persons/objects/words (Autodidasker example); sometimes produces pictures or slight variations akin to modifications in wit. The analogy supports the psychological basis for condensation techniques in wit.
